script.opening: (Karen, talking first:) "Hi doctor, I've booked Sophie in because her acne has got really bad and she's not coping. The over-the-counter stuff isn't working. We need something strong." (Sophie says nothing.)

facts.text: Inflammatory papules and pustules across forehead, cheeks, jawline. A few cystic lesions on chin. Mild scarring forming.
Benzoyl peroxide 5% — caused stinging, gave up. Tea-tree oil. Various Reddit-recommended cleansers.

If the GP can talk to Sophie alone (or asks Sophie directly), she discloses: stopped going to PE. Stopped sleepovers. Has missed school assemblies because of "headaches". Cries before video calls with friends. No active suicidal thoughts but feels hopeless.
Regular. No PCOS features. Not sexually active.
Mother had bad acne until early 20s, treated with isotretinoin. Sophie knows this.

ice.ideas: Sophie thinks it's never going to go away. Karen thinks they need "the same tablet I had".
ice.concerns: Sophie — being judged, falling out with friends. Karen — Sophie's mental health.
ice.expectations: Karen wants isotretinoin. Sophie just wants someone to listen.

cues: Sophie's body language closes off when mum speaks.
Karen interrupts when Sophie tries to answer.

checkpoints.text: Grades the acne (mild/moderate/severe; comedonal vs inflammatory vs nodulocystic)
Starts a structured first-line: topical adapalene + benzoyl peroxide combination, or fixed-combo treatment
Recognises when oral antibiotic (lymecycline) is appropriate; understands when to refer for isotretinoin
Screens for psychological impact — explicitly, not as a tick-box
Creates space for Sophie to speak — asks Karen if it's OK to hear from Sophie directly first
Manages the mother's expectation about isotretinoin without dismissing it
Considers safeguarding the consultation: offers a private follow-up Sophie can attend alone
Safety-nets — mental health worsening, suicidal ideation; signposts (Mind, Kooth, Papyrus HOPELINE247)

worked.txt: "Karen, thank you for booking this. Sophie — would it be OK if I heard from you first, in your own words?"
"Acne isn't just on the skin — it shapes how you walk into a room. Tell me what it's been like for you at school."
"Isotretinoin is brilliant when it's the right answer, but it lives with the specialists. Let's use the first three months really well — that often changes the conversation."
"I'd love to see you again, Sophie, in four weeks — and you're welcome to come on your own if that's easier."
"If you feel hopeless or you start having thoughts of hurting yourself — Papyrus HOPELINE247 is open every day; the number is 0800 068 41 41. And I want you to come and find me."

f.learning: Adolescent acne is almost always also a psychological consultation. The marking failure is letting a parent dominate the airtime and leaving without hearing from the patient themselves. Topical adapalene/BPO is the first-line structure NICE recommends; oral antibiotics are time-limited adjuncts; isotretinoin is consultant-prescribed.

knowledge.summary: Treat with a fixed 12-week topical combination first-line, assess psychological impact explicitly, and remember isotretinoin is specialist-only.

points.t: Offer a 12-week course of a fixed combination: e.g. topical adapalene + benzoyl peroxide, or a topical retinoid + topical antibiotic, or BPO + topical antibiotic. Avoid topical + oral antibiotic together, and don’t use antibiotics as monotherapy.
For moderate–severe disease, add a tetracycline (e.g. lymecycline/doxycycline) with a topical retinoid + BPO; review at 12 weeks, max ~6 months to limit resistance.
Combined oral contraceptive (with a topical agent) is a second-line option, based on contraceptive need and contraindications — not a universal add-on.

Refer to a consultant dermatologist-led team for nodulocystic/conglobate acne, scarring or persistent pigmentation, persistent psychological distress, failure of two completed courses (mild–moderate) or of a course including an oral antibiotic (moderate–severe). Isotretinoin is consultant-initiated with pregnancy-prevention, mental-health and sexual-function safeguards (MHRA).

Acne carries major psychosocial impact; screen mood and function directly. Offer a private review the young person can attend alone, and consider safeguarding; at 16 she is presumed competent to consent (Gillick applies to under-16s).
Signpost Kooth, Mind, and Papyrus HOPELINE247 (0800 068 4141); have a clear plan if mood or self-harm risk worsens.

model.text: Hi Sophie, hi Karen — thanks for joining on video. Sophie, I’d really like to hear from you first: what’s been going on, and how’s it affecting you?
model.why: Addresses the young person directly; open question

model.text: (Sophie) It’s my skin. It’s been getting worse for over a year. I’ve tried face washes and creams from the chemist, nothing works. I hate how I look.
I’m really glad you told me that last part — it matters as much as the spots. Karen, would it be alright if I spent a little time talking just with Sophie at some point? Sometimes it helps.
model.why: Creates space to see the young person alone (Gillick/confidentiality)

model.text: (Karen) Of course. I just want her sorted — my sister swears by those strong tablets.
Sophie, whereabouts is the acne — face, chest, back — and are any of the spots leaving marks or scars?
model.why: Assesses distribution and scarring to grade severity

model.text: (Sophie) Face mostly, some on my back. A few have left little scars, which really upsets me.
Have you tried anything from the GP before, and are your periods regular — any extra hair growth or weight change?
model.why: Prior treatment and a brief PCOS screen

model.text: (Sophie) Nothing from the doctor before. Periods are all over the place, actually.
Thanks — that’s useful and we’ll keep an eye on it. How’s your mood been with all this? Sometimes skin like this really gets people down.
model.why: Screens mood — picks up the psychological impact

model.text: (Sophie) Honestly… not great. I’ve stopped going out. I don’t want people looking at me.
(Gently, with Karen briefly stepped away) Sophie, when you feel that low — have you ever had thoughts of harming yourself?
model.why: Safe, direct risk assessment of low mood

model.text: (Sophie) No, nothing like that. I just feel rubbish about myself.
What’s worried you most about your skin, and what were you hoping for today?
(Sophie) That the scars will be permanent. And I guess I hoped for the strong tablets Mum mentioned.

Let me explain where we are. From what you describe — spots on the face and back with some early scarring — this is moderate acne, and the scarring tells me we shouldn’t be timid. The good news: this is very treatable, and treating it properly is exactly how we prevent more scars.
model.why: Grades severity and explains it in plain language

model.text: (Karen) So can she have the strong tablets?

The very strong tablet your sister means is isotretinoin — it’s a specialist medication with important safety steps, so it’s started by dermatology, not by me. But there’s a lot I can start today that works well, and we don’t have to jump straight there.
model.why: Manages the expectation; explains the isotretinoin route honestly

model.text: What I’d recommend is a combined treatment: a cream that contains a retinoid plus benzoyl peroxide, together with a course of an antibiotic tablet for about twelve weeks. We deliberately combine them — using an antibiotic on its own can breed resistance, so we don’t do that. How does that sound to you, Sophie?
model.why: Correct first-line combination; avoids antibiotic monotherapy

model.text: (Sophie) Okay. Will it sting? I’ve had creams that burned.

It can be drying at first, so we start every other night and build up, with a simple moisturiser — I’ll show you. Give it a good eight to twelve weeks before judging it; skin is slow. And given your irregular periods, the contraceptive pill is another option that can really help acne, if you’d ever want to discuss it.
model.why: Practical adherence advice; offers COC appropriately

model.text: (Sophie) That’s helpful. I’ll try the creams and tablets first.

And on how you’ve been feeling — that matters to me. There are some good resources for young people, like Kooth, that you can use any time, and my door’s open if your mood dips further. You’re not making a fuss.
model.why: Addresses the psychosocial impact within the plan

model.text: I’ll review you at twelve weeks to see how it’s working and decide whether dermatology is the next step — especially to protect against scarring. If your mood ever gets much worse, or you have any thoughts of self-harm, please reach out sooner. Can you tell me the plan back?
model.why: Defined review, scarring/mood safety-net, checks understanding

model.text: (Sophie) Retinoid-and-benzoyl cream plus antibiotic tablets for twelve weeks, build the cream up slowly, and come back in twelve weeks. And I can use Kooth if I’m down.
Perfect. And honestly, Sophie — you’ve done the hard bit by coming. We’ll get on top of this together.

playbook.diagnosis: Grade and explain, then manage expectations: “This is moderate acne, and the early scarring means we shouldn’t be timid — but the very strong tablet is specialist-started with safety steps, and there’s a lot I can start today that works well.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Acne happens when tiny pores get blocked and inflamed — it’s not about being unclean, and it’s very treatable. Treating it well now is exactly how we stop new scars forming, so we’re protecting your skin for the future.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re really worried about scarring, and I’ve heard that — getting on top of this properly now is the best way to prevent more scars, which is exactly what you want.”
management.psychosocial: Name the impact on her mood and confidence; signpost youth support (Kooth/Papyrus) and keep the door open — treat the person, not just the spots.
sharedPlan: 12-week fixed topical combination (e.g. adapalene + benzoyl peroxide); add an oral tetracycline for moderate–severe — never antibiotic monotherapy
Adherence advice (build up slowly, moisturise); offer COC given irregular periods
Review at 12 weeks; dermatology if severe/scarring/failed courses
safetyNet: If mood worsens or any self-harm thoughts → reach out sooner; crisis routes given
Confidentiality + safeguarding handled appropriately for her age

pitfalls.intro: A triadic consultation in disguise: the marks live with the 16-year-old, not the parent — and with the mood screen, not just the prescription.

items.fail: Consulting entirely with the mother — Sophie answers two questions in twelve minutes.
items.why: “Did not engage the young person.” The station exists to test adolescent consulting; every minute spent on Karen’s agenda is a minute of Relating marks unscored.
items.fix: Address Sophie by name from the first minute and make her space explicitly: “Mum, I’ll come to you — but first I’d really like to hear this in Sophie’s words.”

items.fail: Never offering time alone — so mood, bullying and self-harm are asked in front of mum, or not at all.
items.why: “Did not offer a confidential space / apply Gillick.” Sensitive disclosure in front of a parent yields nothing; examiners credit the offer even when it is declined.
items.fix: “Sophie, it’s routine for me to chat with people your age on their own for a couple of minutes — shall we do that now?” Then screen mood directly.

items.fail: Treating the skin and never screening the mind — no questions about mood, school or self-harm despite “I hate how I look”.
items.why: NG198 places psychological impact inside the severity assessment — “failed to assess impact” is a scored Tasks miss, and the cue is scripted to be found.
items.fix: Ask directly and normalise: “Skin like this grinds people down — how has your mood been? Any thoughts of hurting yourself?”

items.fail: An oral antibiotic alone — or a topical antibiotic stacked on an oral one — out of habit from elsewhere.
items.why: NG198 is specific: a 12-week fixed topical combination first-line; never antibiotic monotherapy; never topical plus oral antibiotic together. “Prescribing not in line with UK guidance.”
items.fix: Adapalene + benzoyl peroxide for 12 weeks with expectations set (“often worse before better — we judge it at twelve weeks”), stepping up to lymecycline + topical for moderate–severe disease.

items.fail: “The strong tablets” handled badly at either extreme — a flat “you can’t have isotretinoin”, or a same-day referral to make the consultation easy.
items.why: “Expectation not negotiated.” Isotretinoin is the scripted expectation; both gatekeeping and capitulation lose the negotiation marks.
items.fix: Map the honest path: “That drug exists and it works — it’s specialist-only with serious safeguards. Here’s what has to happen first, and scarring or two failed courses moves us straight there.”

items.fail: A plan whose irritation peak lands in GCSE week — exams never factored in.
items.why: “Plan not tailored to the patient’s context.” Psychosocial information must shape the plan, not decorate the notes.
items.fix: Start low or alternate days through the exams and review after; signpost Kooth; book the 12-week review with Sophie herself, not her mother.

timeMap.d: Karen talks first. Thank her — then ask permission to hear Sophie directly. Whose consultation this becomes is decided in this minute.
Grade the acne (distribution, cysts, scarring). Then the real history: PE stopped, sleepovers stopped, "headaches" before assemblies. Screen mood explicitly, including hopelessness.
"Moderate inflammatory acne with early scarring — and it's costing you school and friends. Both halves deserve treatment."
First-line fixed-combination topical (adapalene/BPO), how to use it, the 6–8 week truth. Address mum's isotretinoin expectation respectfully. Offer Sophie her own follow-up, alone if she prefers.
Mood safety-net with names and numbers (Kooth, Papyrus HOPELINE247). Review at 4 weeks. End by addressing Sophie, not Karen.

wordPics.fail: Conducts the whole consultation with the mother while Sophie says nothing; prescribes (or flatly refuses) isotretinoin territory without explaining the referral structure; never asks about mood despite the body language; no follow-up offered.
wordPics.pass: Gets Sophie talking; grades the acne and starts evidence-based topical treatment; screens psychological impact; explains why isotretinoin is a specialist decision without dismissing Karen; books review with a mood safety-net.
wordPics.exc: Renegotiates the room so Sophie owns the consultation ("could I hear from Sophie first?"); uncovers the school avoidance and names it as the real burden; sets treatment expectations honestly (weeks, purge, sunscreen); offers a confidential solo follow-up; safety-nets hopelessness with specific services and a warm route back.

avoid.dont: "Acne is very common at your age — most people grow out of it."
avoid.instead: "Acne isn't just skin — it decides how you walk into a room. Tell me what it's been costing you."
avoid.why: Normalising dismisses the suffering that brought them in.

avoid.dont: (Only to the mother) "Has she tried anything from the pharmacy?"
avoid.instead: "Karen, thank you — Sophie, would it be OK if I heard it from you first, in your own words?"
avoid.why: Every question routed through the parent silences the actual patient.

avoid.dont: "Isotretinoin is far too dangerous — let's not go there."
avoid.instead: "Isotretinoin is brilliant when it's the right call — and it lives with the specialists. Let's use the next three months so well that we'll know."
avoid.why: Catastrophising the drug dismisses the mother's lived experience of it working.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Grade and explain, then manage expectations: “This is moderate acne, and the early scarring means we shouldn’t be timid — but the very strong tablet is specialist-started with safety steps, and there’s a lot I can start today that works well.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Acne happens when tiny pores get blocked and inflamed — it’s not about being unclean, and it’s very treatable. Treating it well now is exactly how we stop new scars forming, so we’re protecting your skin for the future.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re really worried about scarring, and I’ve heard that — getting on top of this properly now is the best way to prevent more scars, which is exactly what you want.”
management.psychosocial: Name the impact on her mood and confidence; signpost youth support (Kooth/Papyrus) and keep the door open — treat the person, not just the spots.
sharedPlan: 12-week fixed topical combination (e.g. adapalene + benzoyl peroxide); add an oral tetracycline for moderate–severe — never antibiotic monotherapy
Adherence advice (build up slowly, moisturise); offer COC given irregular periods
Review at 12 weeks; dermatology if severe/scarring/failed courses
safetyNet: If mood worsens or any self-harm thoughts → reach out sooner; crisis routes given
Confidentiality + safeguarding handled appropriately for her age

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: A triadic consultation in disguise: the marks live with the 16-year-old, not the parent — and with the mood screen, not just the prescription.

items.fail: Consulting entirely with the mother — Sophie answers two questions in twelve minutes.
items.why: “Did not engage the young person.” The station exists to test adolescent consulting; every minute spent on Karen’s agenda is a minute of Relating marks unscored.
items.fix: Address Sophie by name from the first minute and make her space explicitly: “Mum, I’ll come to you — but first I’d really like to hear this in Sophie’s words.”

items.fail: Never offering time alone — so mood, bullying and self-harm are asked in front of mum, or not at all.
items.why: “Did not offer a confidential space / apply Gillick.” Sensitive disclosure in front of a parent yields nothing; examiners credit the offer even when it is declined.
items.fix: “Sophie, it’s routine for me to chat with people your age on their own for a couple of minutes — shall we do that now?” Then screen mood directly.

items.fail: Treating the skin and never screening the mind — no questions about mood, school or self-harm despite “I hate how I look”.
items.why: NG198 places psychological impact inside the severity assessment — “failed to assess impact” is a scored Tasks miss, and the cue is scripted to be found.
items.fix: Ask directly and normalise: “Skin like this grinds people down — how has your mood been? Any thoughts of hurting yourself?”

items.fail: An oral antibiotic alone — or a topical antibiotic stacked on an oral one — out of habit from elsewhere.
items.why: NG198 is specific: a 12-week fixed topical combination first-line; never antibiotic monotherapy; never topical plus oral antibiotic together. “Prescribing not in line with UK guidance.”
items.fix: Adapalene + benzoyl peroxide for 12 weeks with expectations set (“often worse before better — we judge it at twelve weeks”), stepping up to lymecycline + topical for moderate–severe disease.

items.fail: “The strong tablets” handled badly at either extreme — a flat “you can’t have isotretinoin”, or a same-day referral to make the consultation easy.
items.why: “Expectation not negotiated.” Isotretinoin is the scripted expectation; both gatekeeping and capitulation lose the negotiation marks.
items.fix: Map the honest path: “That drug exists and it works — it’s specialist-only with serious safeguards. Here’s what has to happen first, and scarring or two failed courses moves us straight there.”

items.fail: A plan whose irritation peak lands in GCSE week — exams never factored in.
items.why: “Plan not tailored to the patient’s context.” Psychosocial information must shape the plan, not decorate the notes.
items.fix: Start low or alternate days through the exams and review after; signpost Kooth; book the 12-week review with Sophie herself, not her mother.
